claims.statement: Self-relevant information recruits top-down appraisal systems capable of biasing attentional processing toward personally significant stimuli.
Affective evaluations of goodness/badness can serve as information in judgment and decision making, forming the basis of the affect heuristic.
Matching persuasive messages to recipients' motivational orientations produces a small but reliable persuasion advantage across many experimental tests, with meaningful moderators.
Social identity and accommodation processes can shape linguistic choices and communicative style, while language cues can also index social identities.
Evaluative polarity in wording can contribute to risky-choice framing effects, showing that lexical/connotative properties can help construct decision frames.
Structural and grammatical message variables can alter persuasion through their effects on processing, but direction and magnitude depend on elaboration and context.
